> **What this case shows** — the clinic measures *capacity* (what an arm **can**
> do on command); daily life reveals *performance* (what it **actually** does).
> These come apart, and the wearable **use ratio** and **magnitude ratio**
> quantify the gap between the two arms. On real dual-arm accelerometry from a
> healthy person the ecosystem recovers the **symmetric reference**: whenever the
> arms are in use, **both** are used near-equally — every one of the **14 dynamic
> activities** has a **|magnitude ratio| < 0.5** (max **0.34**, mean **0.12**) and
> a use ratio of **1.0**, and the overall magnitude ratio is **−0.05** (0 =
> symmetric). This is the healthy baseline against which the stroke
> affected/unaffected asymmetry — use ratio far below 1, magnitude ratio strongly
> negative — is read. **What reproduces, and what doesn't** — the *symmetry*
> reproduces on the freely public data; the *clinical asymmetry* needs
> bilateral-**wrist** recordings from an impaired cohort (DUA-gated), so it is the
> documented target application, not a claim made here. **How to read it** — left,
> per-activity arm-use symmetry (bars near zero = both arms used equally); right,
> the overall symmetric use.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — from two limb-worn accelerometers, compute the **use ratio**
(active hours of one arm ÷ the other) and the **magnitude ratio** (log ratio of
per-epoch activity), summarising *how symmetric* everyday arm use is.
**Way of thinking** — a wearable measures **performance**, not capacity; the
clinically meaningful quantity is the *gap between the arms*, and its natural
zero is healthy **symmetry** — so validate the metric by showing it *recovers
symmetry* where symmetry is expected, before trusting the asymmetry it reports in
patients.
**Ecosystem usage** — `upperLimbUse()` (PhysioWearable) on right/left
accelerometer streams from any reader.
:::

## Proposition

Capacity and performance are different things, and the use ratio / magnitude ratio
measure the gap. On real dual-arm accelerometry from a healthy person the ecosystem
recovers the symmetric reference — every dynamic activity has |magnitude ratio| <
0.5 (max **0.34**, mean **0.12**), use ratio **1.0**, overall magnitude ratio
**−0.05** — the baseline against which stroke asymmetry is measured.

## Question & goal

**The question is a capacity-versus-performance one.** Upper-limb rehabilitation
has long known that what a patient *can* do in a five-minute clinic assessment is
not what the arm *does* over a day at home. Wrist-worn accelerometry made the
second thing measurable: Bailey, Lang and Uswatte defined the **use ratio** (how
long the affected arm is active relative to the unaffected) and the **magnitude
ratio** (how *hard* each arm works), whose natural zero point is healthy
**symmetry**. We ask: on real two-arm accelerometry, does `upperLimbUse()` recover
that symmetric reference?

## Challenge & approach

The metric is only trustworthy in patients if it reads *symmetric* where symmetry
is real. We take a healthy subject's **right-arm and left-arm** accelerometers
across 19 daily and sports activities, convert to *g*, and run `upperLimbUse()` per
activity and overall. The honest reading separates two regimes: **dynamic**
activities, where both arms cross the movement threshold and symmetry is
meaningful, and **static** ones (sitting, lying), where the arms barely move and
the ratio is undefined-by-inactivity rather than asymmetry.

## Data

**DSADS** (Barshan & Altun, UCI #256) — five IMUs including a right-arm and a
left-arm unit at 25 Hz, 19 activities × 60 five-second segments per subject.
Accelerometry in m/s² → *g*. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Per-activity arm-use symmetry for the 14 activities in which both arms are used
(left; bars within ±0.5 = symmetric, all are), and the overall symmetric use
(right).](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* on the left, each bar is one activity's magnitude ratio (log
right/left activity); every dynamic activity sits within ±0.5 of zero — both arms
work near-equally, the healthy symmetric pattern. On the right, the overall use
ratio (0.86, pulled below 1 only by the static activities where neither arm is
used) and the near-zero overall magnitude ratio.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| overall use ratio (1 = symmetric) | **0.86** |
| overall magnitude ratio (0 = symmetric) | **−0.05** |
| activities with both arms in use | **14** |
| largest per-activity \|magnitude ratio\| (all < 0.5) | **0.34** |
| mean per-activity \|magnitude ratio\| | **0.12** |

## Conclusion

On real dual-arm data the use ratio and magnitude ratio recover exactly what a
healthy body should show — **both arms used, near-equally, whenever the arms are
used at all**. The transferable takeaway: **a wearable measures performance, not
capacity, and the clinically meaningful signal is the gap between the arms —
validate the metric by confirming it recovers symmetry in the unimpaired before
trusting the asymmetry it reports in patients.**

## Open questions

- The clinical capacity-performance gap — affected-arm use ratio well below 1 and
  a strongly negative magnitude ratio in stroke or cerebral palsy — needs
  bilateral-**wrist** recordings from an impaired cohort (e.g. NICHD DASH). Those
  are data-use-agreement gated, not freely public, so this case validates the
  method against the healthy symmetric reference and documents the clinical
  asymmetry as the target application. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| step | function | package |
|---|---|---|
| read two limb accelerometer streams | any reader → matrices | PhysioWearable |
| use ratio + magnitude ratio + laterality | `upperLimbUse()` | PhysioWearable |

**Choosing the parameters:** pass the **affected** arm first and the **unaffected**
second (in the clinic that is contralesional/ipsilesional; here right/left),
`sampling_rate` and `epoch_sec` to match your device, and read the **use ratio**
(1 = symmetric, → 0 as one arm drops out) with the **magnitude ratio** (0 =
symmetric, negative = the first arm works less) *together* — one counts *whether*
the arm is used, the other *how hard*. Interpret only over epochs where the body
is active; static periods are undefined-by-inactivity, not asymmetry.

```r
library(PhysioWearable)
u <- upperLimbUse(right_arm_acc, left_arm_acc, sampling_rate = 25, epoch_sec = 5)
u$use_ratio        # 1 = symmetric; << 1 = the first arm is used far less
u$magnitude_ratio  # 0 = symmetric; < 0 = the first arm works less hard
```

One line for the technical reader: every number traces to
[`artifacts/overall_use.csv`](artifacts/overall_use.csv) and
[`artifacts/per_activity_use.csv`](artifacts/per_activity_use.csv), re-checked by
[`audit.py`](audit.py) and `tools/validate_case.py`.
